channel.title: iRecord Updates
channel.description: Updates for iRecord - Professional screen recording

item.title: Version 1.228.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.228.0

Added

  • A recording that doesn't finish is offered back to you next time you open iRecord — if the app or your Mac stopped unexpectedly mid-recording, the file used to be unplayable and iRecord never mentioned it existed. Recordings are now written so that everything up to the last few seconds survives, and the next launch asks whether you want it back. Choosing to discard keeps the files for a week in case you didn't mean it.
  • The recording indicator shows how much is already safe on disk — a second line under the timer, so you can see the recording is being written and not just counting. For the first few seconds it reads --:--, because nothing has been written yet and saying 00:00 looked like something had gone wrong.

Fixed

  • The recording timer no longer freezes while a menu is open — opening a menu, or dragging the recording indicator around the screen, stopped the clock for as long as you held it there, and then it jumped forward when you let go. The recording itself was always fine; only the counter stalled. It now keeps time from the clock rather than by counting its own ticks, so it stays right even when the Mac is busy.
  • The mouse pointer is still tracked while a menu is open — the same fault affected the pointer trail behind the zoom effect, which stopped being recorded for as long as any menu was down. That left a gap at the exact moment the pointer was most likely to be moving.
  • Recordings you add or remove in Finder now show up on the Home screen — the list was read once when iRecord started, so a Recording folder you deleted in Finder kept appearing, and one you moved in never showed at all until you quit and reopened the app. Home now checks for changes when you go back to it and when you switch back to iRecord.
  • A recording that didn't finish now says when it stopped, not just when it started — the offer to bring it back gave the length and the start time, so there was no way to tell a recording that ended early from one that ran until the Mac did.
  • Running out of disk space mid-recording now stops and saves instead of silently breaking the take — the check only ran before you pressed Record, so a long recording could outrun the space it started with and end up damaged with nothing said. iRecord now warns while there is still room to free some up, and if space runs out anyway it stops and saves what you have.
  • A take with no picture no longer breaks the whole recording — the app used to pick a take that saved sound but no video, and then your video wouldn't save at all. Those takes are skipped now, and a recording already stuck this way fixes itself when you open it. Nothing is deleted.
  • The camera stays in step with an iPhone or iPad recording after the cable is knocked — when the connection dropped and came back, the app trimmed the dead air out of the phone recording but not out of the camera in the corner. Your face then ran behind your voice for the rest of the take, by however long the cable was out. The camera now pauses with the recording and picks up in the right place.
  • Recordings on the home screen no longer sit on top of each other — each card was being stretched to the size of the picture inside it, so they came out at different widths and overlapped their neighbours. Every recording now gets an evenly sized card with the picture trimmed to fit.

item.title: Version 1.224.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.224.0

Added

  • Reorder the sections of a recording without re-recording them — select a block on the timeline and press ⌥← or ⌥→ to move it one place earlier or later. The pricing bit can come before the demo after the fact. ⌘Z puts the order back exactly as it was, and the saved video follows the order you see. Dragging blocks to reorder is still to come; the keyboard works today.

Fixed

  • ⌘Z while renaming a recording now undoes what you typed — it used to reach past the name field and undo your last trim or split instead, which is the opposite of what a text field is expected to do. Renaming also no longer lets ⌘B or ⌘K cut the timeline mid-word.
  • Cancelling "Record next section" no longer leaves an empty section behind — the section had to be created before the recorder could roll, and backing out of the source picker left it in the recording for good, silently pushing the numbering along each time. Backing out now leaves the recording exactly as it was, however the recording failed to start.
  • The Ready screen tells you screen recording access is needed before you press Record — macOS takes that permission back every so often on its own, and the app only found out at the moment capture started, after the countdown. It is now checked when the Ready screen opens and every time you switch back to iRecord, so the Grant row is on screen before you pick anything, alongside a line saying that macOS re-asks periodically and this is not iRecord losing your permission. On a Mac where access had been revoked, that same check used to take about eighteen seconds and let the system raise its own dialog on top; it is now immediate and silent.
  • Recording a specific window could fail instantly, every time — picking a window from Ready and hitting Record threw "Failed to setup capture session" before the countdown even started. The window list had been widened to show windows on other Spaces or behind other apps, but the check that runs when Record is actually pressed was never updated to match, so it could never find the window the list had just offered. The two now agree.
  • Record could run its countdown and fail on a microphone permission it already knew was missing — with Microphone switched on but not yet granted, the Grant row said so right there in the same screen, but Record stayed enabled and only failed after the countdown, with a raw system error instead of pointing at the row.

Changed

  • The quality row on Save Video reads as a control now, not a caption — "High Quality — Best quality · Larger file ⌄ Advanced" was plain text next to a chevron, with no chrome telling you it opened anything. It now has the same button chip and hover state as the rest of the sheet, and the "Advanced" label and chevron sit together at the trailing edge, which is where a disclosure control is expected.

item.title: Version 1.223.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.223.0

Fixed

  • The camera stays live when the screen holds still, in the editor and in the saved video alike — if you talked over a slide, a document or any window you weren't touching, the camera in the corner froze for as long as the screen didn't change, then jumped back to life the moment it did. The recording of your screen and your voice were both fine; only the camera stopped. It was being recorded one frame per change on screen, and a screen that isn't changing produces none — so a recording that sat still for three minutes lost three minutes of your face. Saving had the same fault a second time over, so even a good recording came out of Save Video frozen. The camera now records on its own clock, and a saved video keeps a steady picture no matter how still your screen is. Recordings already made cannot be repaired: the frames were never captured. Saving one of them will now play the frames it does have at a steady rate, but it cannot invent the missing ones.

item.title: Version 1.222.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.222.0

Fixed

  • Saving a long recording no longer fails with "Cannot Decode" — past a certain length, saving stopped partway and reported two words that explained nothing. Your recording was never damaged: the app was decoding your footage several times over at once — once to save it, and again to keep the preview and the camera running behind the Save screen — while holding on to frames it had finished with. macOS eventually shut the decoder down, which the app reported as being unable to read your video. It now stops the preview while saving and releases frames as it uses them. This was never about a particular Mac; it reproduced on one with twice the memory. Saving also got faster: the shape used to round the camera's corners was being redrawn for every frame instead of once, and the progress bar was being updated fifty thousand times.
  • A save that loses frames says so — if a Mac ran short of memory mid-save, frames could be dropped and the video would come out shorter than the canvas with nothing said about it. That can no longer pass in silence.
  • The preview stops when a save starts — it used to keep playing, and keep decoding the same footage, for the whole export.

Changed

  • A failed update now leaves evidence behind — when an update would not install, nothing was written down anywhere, so the only account of it was the customer's memory of a dialog. Sparkle's download, install and failure steps now go into the app's log, naming the reason the way the developers of Sparkle name it rather than as a bare number, and a diagnostics report picks them up. The report also says where iRecord is installed and whether it can update itself from there — an app still running from its disk image, or from a copy macOS has quarantined, cannot replace itself no matter how many times you check for updates, and neither state looks wrong from the outside. Drag iRecord to Applications and it can.

item.title: Version 1.221.0
item.description:
What's New in 1.221.0

Changed

  • The timeline zooms out to the whole recording, and in to a single frame — a long recording could not be seen end to end at any zoom, and could not be zoomed in far enough to place a cut on a frame. The zoom-out end now means "everything, in one screen", whatever the recording's length, and the zoom-in end reaches frame level. The editor opens showing the whole thing, Fit returns to it in one click, the two magnifiers step in and out, and zooming keeps the playhead where your eye already is instead of scrolling out from under you. Long timelines also stay smooth while you do it.
  • Picking a window tells you what each window is — the grid was ragged, and windows that could not be previewed all came out as the same grey rectangle, so four different windows read as one app repeated. Every window now shows its app icon — instead of the preview when there isn't one, beside it when there is — with the window title and the app it belongs to on every card. A line under the grid explains what the list contains: windows from every desktop and Space, which is why some have no preview and all of them are still recordable.
  • The camera's Fine-tune settings are easier to find, and easier to skip — the row that opens position, size, shape and border was the faintest thing in the panel while being the door to all of it. It now reads as a control, and when closed it shows what it is hiding, so checking your framing costs nothing.
  • A new recording's camera has no white ring — the border was 2 px by default, a styling opinion applied to footage nobody had looked at yet. It now starts at 0 and the slider is there when you want one. Recordings you have already made are untouched.
  • Reporting a problem now brings the evidence with it — Help → "Report an Issue…" gathers a diagnostics file, shows it to you in Finder, and opens an email ready to send. Attach the file and the report arrives with your macOS version, Mac model, free disk space, permission states and the app's own log, instead of "it didn't work". Nothing is sent anywhere on its own: the file is written to your Mac, you read it, and you decide whether to attach it. It contains no video and no licence key.

Fixed

  • A failed save says where it failed — an export that could not read part of a recording reported two words, "Cannot Decode", with no indication of what had gone wrong or where. It now names the point in the video it stopped at, so a damaged stretch of one take is identifiable instead of looking like a broken app.
